posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Can some one describe what the mode hopping fringes look like. I hear it compared to sliced bread but does that mean the fringes always slice the object from top to bottom or sided to side? Is is possible the sliced bread look can be from the front of the object (closest to plate) to the back of the object?

Unfortunately (or fortunately actually), I have never seen mode hopping fringes first hand.

It would be really great if a short video or a few pics could be posted.

Thanks in advance, 

John

posts.author: Kris Meerlo
posts.content_md:
Hi John,

Look here [http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=5342](http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=5342) I posted a video of a mode hop.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: The banding is in planes parrallel to the plate. More precicely they are spheres with the radius from the pinhole as the center.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: Ah, thank you so very kindly Kris. That is exactly what I am looking for.

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** The banding is in planes parallel to the plate. More precisely they are spheres with the radius from the pinhole as the center.

OK Colin but can you or anyone explain the following observation please? 

Using a green 20mw laser pointer running off a 3Volt stabilized dc power supply I get a holo with classic sharp dark fringes (about 7) off a 

well-polished 1 inch diameter coin which is replaying to the viewer almost on axis as a specular reflector just half an inch away from plate. BUT in the same hologram coins that are 3 inches away or more from plate at non -specularly reflecting angles resting on a bright diffuse surface dont show any sliced bread effect and work pretty well ! What do you reckon is going on?

Jeff

posts.content_md:
I will take a stab at this:

If the fringes do not overrun the edge of the coin in question, then I think the coin moved or changed shape, for some reason, during exposure. Everything else was stable, and the laser did not mode hop. If the laser did not mode hop, what model and brand was it and how did you luck out in getting it??

This is a very interesting and potentially useful observation! Diffuse illumination of the object seems to somehow smear out the contour lines so they are invisible! Or much less visible, anyway. I can sort of imagine how this might be the case, but then when I think about what kind of fringes to expect from a diffusely illuminated, diffusely reflecting object, even with a single line laser, my brain hurts and I must lie down.

posts.author: walschuler
posts.content_md: So, Jeff, did my email above capture the appearance of your case? If so, why get involved at all with specular vs. diffuse, or angle of reflection? It seems to me the suggestion I made works. I see such things in my students' holograms with some frequency. Dealing with object stability cures the problem.
